subject: English
name: English, Year 10
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: English, Level 10

points.title: Inclusive and exclusive language
points.brief: Language can draw people in, as with we and our, or shut them out, as with jargon, in-jokes and talk of us and them.

points.title: Language that empowers or disempowers
points.brief: Labels, the names given to groups and who is made the subject of a sentence can give people dignity and agency or take them away.

points.title: Implicit and explicit evaluation
points.brief: Writers judge openly with clear opinion words, or quietly through connotation and which details they include, and both reveal their values.

points.title: Judging how well a structure works
points.brief: Evaluating a structure means asking whether its order, sections and paragraphing help the text achieve its purpose for its audience.

points.title: Frames and circular structures
points.brief: A frame story sits inside another, and a circular structure ends where it began, both creating links that make readers compare start and end.

points.title: Cohesion across an extended essay
points.brief: An introduction that maps the argument, topic sentences that echo it and linking words between paragraphs hold a long essay together.

points.title: Syntax and style
points.brief: Syntax is the order of words in a sentence. Moving a phrase to the front or holding the main point to the end changes emphasis and style.

points.title: Parallel structure
points.brief: Repeating the same grammatical pattern across a list or a pair of clauses gives balance and rhythm and makes ideas easy to compare.

points.title: Active and passive voice
points.brief: The active voice says who did an action. The passive voice puts the action first and can hide who did it, as in mistakes were made.

points.title: Shades of meaning
points.brief: Choosing the most precise word from a group of near synonyms, such as ask, request, demand and plead, gives exactly the meaning intended.

points.title: Punctuation for rhythm and effect
points.brief: Writers use punctuation on purpose to control pace and emphasis, such as an ellipsis for hesitation or a single-word sentence for impact.

points.title: Mise en scene
points.brief: Everything placed in the frame, such as setting, costume, props, lighting and where actors stand, which together build meaning in a shot.

points.title: Editing choices in film
points.brief: The order and length of shots, cuts, montage and slow motion change how viewers understand people and events on screen.

points.title: Documentary techniques
points.brief: Interviews, archival footage, voice-over and the choice of who speaks shape how a documentary represents its subject.

points.title: How a text reflects its context
points.brief: Evaluating how a text's attitudes, assumptions and representations of people and places reflect the time and culture it came from.

points.title: Reading Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature in context
points.brief: Texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors are best read with attention to the author's community and history, and to cultures that continue today.

points.title: Building an interpretation
points.brief: An interpretation is a reasoned view of what a text means, built from patterns of evidence across the whole text.

points.title: Other readings of a text
points.brief: Readers can interpret the same text differently, such as by focusing on power, gender or history, and weighing other readings sharpens your own.

points.title: Ethical dilemmas in literature
points.brief: Literature often puts characters in situations with no easy right answer, which invites readers to weigh competing values.

points.title: Voice as a literary device
points.brief: A writer builds a voice through diction, rhythm, attitude and point of view, and a distinct voice can make readers trust, pity or doubt a speaker.

points.title: Comparing voice across texts
points.brief: Setting two voices side by side shows how different choices of word, sentence and attitude create different emotional effects.

points.title: Parody, pastiche and homage
points.brief: A parody copies a text's style to mock it, a pastiche imitates a style playfully, and an homage borrows from a text to honour it.

points.title: How endings shape interpretation
points.brief: A text's ending, whether resolved, open or twisting, changes how readers understand everything before it.

points.title: Keeping a voice consistent
points.brief: A sustained voice keeps the same viewpoint, vocabulary and attitude throughout, so the speaker feels real from start to finish.

points.title: Transforming a text into a new form
points.brief: Retelling a text in another form or from another character's view, such as a monologue or a letter, changes what readers notice and feel.

points.title: The dramatic monologue
points.brief: A dramatic monologue is one character speaking to a silent listener, revealing more about themselves than they mean to.

points.title: Supporting a view in discussion
points.brief: In discussion, a strong contribution states a view about a text, backs it with an example, and responds to what others have said.

points.title: Choosing the level of formality
points.brief: A speaker may mix formal and informal language on purpose, such as a casual story inside a formal speech, to connect with an audience.

points.title: Evaluating representations of concepts
points.brief: Judging how fairly and fully a text represents a concept such as success or justice, and how that reflects its context.

points.title: Playing with spelling for effect
points.brief: Advertisers, poets and brands bend standard spelling on purpose to catch the eye or create a sound, which works only when the standard form is known.

points.title: Implicit values
points.brief: A text can carry values without stating them, through what it treats as normal, who it centres and what it leaves out.

points.title: Irony and satire
points.brief: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or happens. Satire uses irony and humour to criticise people or society.

points.title: Organising ideas for a purpose
points.brief: Analysing why a writer orders ideas as they do, such as saving the strongest point for last or opening with a story, and judging how well it works.

points.title: Inferring themes
points.brief: A theme is an idea about life that a text explores, worked out by inference from patterns in its characters, conflicts and symbols.

points.title: Writing a thesis statement
points.brief: A thesis statement gives a clear, arguable answer to the question in one or two sentences, and the essay goes on to prove it.

points.title: Integrating evidence and analysis
points.brief: Good analysis embeds short quotations, names the technique, and explains how it creates meaning, rather than retelling the plot.

points.title: Refining an analytical essay
points.brief: Refining checks that every paragraph supports the thesis, evidence is explained, expression is concise, and the conclusion does more than repeat.
